newsitem.title: UK: UK biotech hit by AutoImmune failure.
newsitem.headline: UK biotech hit by AutoImmune failure.

text.p: Fall-out from the failure of a new U.S. biotech drug hit Britain's fast-growing biotechnology sector on Tuesday, analysts said.
News on Monday that late-stage trials showed that AutoImmune Inc's lead drug for treating multiple sclerosis, Myloral, was no better than a placebo caused AutoImmune's shares to plunge.
The stock fell 68 percent to $4-5/16 on Monday, and helped to drag the jittery U.S. biotech sector down by around five percent overall.

Falls in stocks in the UK biotech sector on Tuesday were uneven, with most of the heat being felt by companies which are about to publish important late-stage drug data, notably Celltech Group Plc and Cortecs International Plc.

While the biotechs sagged, shares in conventional drug majors including Glaxo Wellcome Plc, SmithKline Beecham Plc and Zeneca Group Plc all rose. Analysts said the AutoImmune failure, which follows a string of high profile disappointments in the U.S, underlined the inherent riskiness of biotech investments.
The less mature British sector, which is by far Europe's largest, now stands at a crucial stage, with a number of leading companies preparing to launch their first products.

"This is a confidence-based sector and confidence has taken a bit of a tumble," said Yamaichi International analyst Erling Refsum. But he added: "That is probably the best time to buy - people are valuing this with their hearts not their heads."
Refsum said AutoImmune had "pushed its product faster than was warranted," going ahead with Phase III trials before Phase I and II had been properly completed.
Falls in the UK "were an overreaction, but the sector is subject to that," he added.

Shares in Celltech, which is expected to announce Phase III results of a septic shock drug under development with Germany's Bayer AG in the next few weeks, were down 24-1/2 pence at 560 pence midmorning, while Cortecs, which is about to publish results on its oral osteoporosis treatment Macritonin, were down 12 pence at 260.

Analysts said Celltech may also have been hurt by Eli Lilley & Co's statement on Monday that the cardiovascular drug ReoPro, on which Celltech receives a royalty, may not continue to grow at the rate seen in the first quarter.
But Lehman Brothers analyst Ian Smith said nervousness about data on BAYX-1351 for septic shock, due in the next few weeks, was the key to the price fall.

Smith said Celltech's shares had an upside of two pounds ($3.26) on good news and a downside of a similar amount on bad, but added "I am very comfortable about the outcome, so any weakness here is a buying opportunity."
Anglo-Australian Cortecs is also preparing to announce Phase III results, possibly this week, on a tablet form of Calcitonin, a drug for treating the bone-wasting disease osteoporosis.
A number of analysts, including Yamaichi's Refsum and Nomura's Nick Woolf, believe positive results will push the group's share price through the 400 pence barrier.

But Lehman's Smith is more cautious. He said good news would add around 75 pence to Cortecs shares, but disappointment could see it plunge by more than 60 percent to below 100 pence. He said investors should wait for the data before putting new money in, "or take money out of the stock."

The sector's flagship stock, British Biotech Plc, was little troubled by the AutoImmune debacle, losing just 2-1/2 pence to 235. The company is not due to publish Phase III data on its main product, cancer treatment Marimastat, until next year.

Rare bright spots in the sector were PPL Therapeutics Plc, maker of Dolly the world's most famous sheep, which rose 2 1/2 to 386, and Innovative Technology Group Plc, up 1 at 332, which predicted strong growth for its range of biomaterials on Tuesday. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
